query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu coatings operating under high‐temperature sliding conditions, the overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation are governed by the formation of an adherent, protective copper oxide layer. This oxide layer forms preferentially from Cu that segregates to the grain boundaries during a controlled annealing treatment and, once formed during high-temperature use, reduces direct metal–metal contact and alters the dominant deformation mechanism away from dislocation‐mediated plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a conventional metal substrate with a nanocrystalline, chemically homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled annealing treatment (relative to the as-deposited baseline) designed to promote Cu segregation to grain boundaries, thereby setting the stage for in situ oxidation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in ambient atmosphere at high temperatures (around 300°C and above) where oxidation reactions are active.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a continuous and adherent Cu oxide layer at the surface and along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Annealing enhances Cu segregation. Under high-temperature sliding, the segregated Cu oxidizes to form a lubricious, protective film that reduces direct asperity contact, inhibits dislocation and grain-boundary mediated plastic deformation, and thereby lowers friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that receive the controlled annealing treatment should exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to as-deposited coatings, along with microscopic evidence of a shift from dislocation-dominated deformation to deformation mediated by the presence of a protective oxide layer.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without additional annealing, which is expected to have less pronounced Cu segregation and oxide formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-temperature sliding conditions (≈300°C and above) in ambient atmospheric environments that support oxidation reactions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of friction and wear rate reduction is uncertain, as it depends on the degree of Cu segregation and oxide film quality. Additional quantitative testing is required to determine precise effect sizes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated substrates: one set as-deposited (control) and one set subjected to a controlled annealing treatment intended to promote Cu segregation. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests at around 300°C under ambient conditions. Characterize the surfaces post-test using techniques such as XPS, SEM, or TEM to detect the presence and continuity of Cu oxides and use tribological measurements to record friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Friction coefficient during sliding wear tests
Wear rate (e.g., volume loss per unit distance and load)
Surface and cross-sectional chemical composition (with focus on Cu oxide formation) via XPS/EDS
Microstructural analysis of deformation mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary vs dislocation activities)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a significant enrichment of Cu oxides compared to the as-deposited samples, or if they fail to exhibit a measurable reduction in friction and wear rate or a shift in the deformation mechanism, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
